2027-06-25.title: Sixth Friday of the Apostles
2027-06-25.readTitle: Readings of the day (First Set; mapped from the official calendar, verify locally)
readings: Give to the emperor what is the emperor's, and to God what is God's
2027-06-25.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and from Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed again in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar's own headings: “All powers are from God”; “Give to Caesar what is to him”.
2027-06-25.verse: They answered, “The emperor’s.” Then he said to them, “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
theo: In the last week of the Season of the Apostles the readings turn to a question that every disciple faces in the street, in the office and at the ballot box: how does a Christian live under earthly government? The Gospel begins with a trap. “Then the Pharisees went and plotted to entrap him in what he said.” They send their disciples together with the Herodians, the party that supported the house of Herod and therefore Roman rule. The two groups did not normally agree, but they agree now against Jesus. They begin with flattery: “Teacher, we know that you are sincere, and teach the way of God in accordance with truth, and show deference to no one.” Then the question: “Is it lawful to pay taxes to the emperor, or not?” If Jesus says yes, he loses the crowds who hate the Roman tax; if he says no, the Herodians can report him to the governor as a rebel. Jesus, “aware of their malice”, asks for the coin used for the tax. They produce a denarius. The detail matters: they carry Caesar's coin, with Caesar's image and an inscription calling him a son of a god, even into the precincts of the Temple. “Whose head is this, and whose title?” “The emperor’s.” “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”

The answer is not a clever escape. It draws a line through every human life. The coin bears the emperor's image, so give it back to him: pay what is due, take part in the life of the city, respect the law. But the human person bears another image. “So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them” (Genesis 1:27). If the coin belongs to the one whose image it carries, then you belong wholly to God, whose image you carry. Caesar may ask for taxes; he may not ask for your soul. The early Christians lived exactly this way. They paid taxes and prayed for the emperors, but they refused to offer incense before the emperor's statue, and many died for that refusal. Peter and the apostles, who will be honoured on Tuesday, had already said it before the council in Jerusalem: “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29).

Paul's letter to the Romans, written to Christians living in the capital of the empire, gives the other side of the teaching. “Let every person be subject to the governing authorities; for there is no authority except from God, and those authorities that exist have been instituted by God.” Paul is not praising Nero, nor saying that every ruler is good. He is saying that order in society, law, courts and public service are part of God's providence for human life; without them the weak are devoured by the strong. The ruler is “God’s servant for your good”. That phrase is both an honour and a judgment: authority exists for the good of the people, and it will answer to God for how it serves. Then comes a very ordinary instruction: “For the same reason you also pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s servants, busy with this very thing.” Honest taxes, honest bills, no bribe to the officer and no bribe taken from the citizen: these are part of Christian holiness. Paul adds that we obey “not only because of wrath but also because of conscience”. A Christian is honest not only when a camera is watching but because God sees.

For Christians in India this teaching is very practical. We live in a great democracy, among neighbours of many faiths. We are called to be good citizens: to vote with a formed conscience, to pay our taxes, to keep the traffic rules, to refuse the small corruption that has become normal, and to serve in public office with clean hands. At the same time we pray for those in authority, as Paul asked Timothy to pray “for kings and all who are in high positions, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceable life in all godliness and dignity” (1 Timothy 2:2). And when a law or an order commands what God forbids, the Christian answers with Peter and with the martyrs: God first. On this Friday of the Season of the Apostles let us give back to Caesar the coin, and give back to God ourselves.
outline: A coin in the hand: whose image is on it, and whose image is on me?
Point 1 · All authority is from God
Order and law as God's providence; the ruler as God's servant for the good of the people.
Point 2 · Give to God what is God's
We bear God's image: we belong wholly to him.
Honest citizens, praying for rulers, and God first when a law commands sin.
“Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s.”
live: Check one area this week where you may be cutting corners: a tax, a bill, a ticket, a small bribe. Put it right.
Before sleep each night this week, offer the whole day back to God in a short prayer: “All that I am is yours.”
fathers: We pay the taxes and contributions to those appointed by you before all others, as Christ taught us. We worship God alone, but in other things we gladly serve you, acknowledging you as rulers and praying that with royal power you may also be found to have sound judgment.

Caesar looks for his image on the coin; God looks for his image in you. As Caesar demands his coin back, so God demands back the soul he has stamped with his likeness. Give Caesar his money; give God yourself.
magis: Those subject to authority should regard those in authority as representatives of God; their loyal collaboration includes the right, and at times the duty, to voice their just criticisms of what seems harmful to the dignity of persons and the good of the community.
Submission to authority and co-responsibility for the common good make it morally obligatory to pay taxes, to exercise the right to vote and to defend one's country.

The citizen is obliged in conscience not to follow the directives of civil authorities when they are contrary to the demands of the moral order, to the fundamental rights of persons or the teachings of the Gospel: we must obey God rather than men.
saints: Sixth Friday of the Apostles. June is the month of the Sacred Heart in popular devotion; many families pray the litany of the Sacred Heart in the evening prayer this month.

25–30 June: sixth and seventh weeks of the Season of the Apostles. Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles, the last Sunday of the season. Mon 28: St Irenaeus, bishop and martyr (also a memorial in the Latin calendar). Tue 29: St Peter and St Paul, the Apostles, an important feast and a day of obligation. Wed 30: in the Latin calendar, the First Martyrs of the Holy Roman Church. Looking ahead: the Dukhrana of St Thomas, our Father in faith, on Saturday 3 July, and the Season of Kaitha (Qaita) from Sunday 4 July.
2027-06-25.prayer: Lord God, you are the source of all authority, and every human being bears your image. Bless our country and all who govern it, from the village panchayat to the Parliament; give them wisdom, honesty and a care for the poor. Make us good citizens, honest in our taxes and duties and faithful to our conscience. Keep us from every form of corruption, and give us courage, like your apostles and martyrs, to obey you first when the world asks what you forbid. We give back to you ourselves, made in your image, through Jesus Christ our Lord, who with you and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns, for ever. Amen.
altar: At the Holy Qurbana we place on the altar bread and wine, and with them our work, our earnings and our citizenship. The coin belongs to Caesar, but the offering of ourselves belongs to God, and in the Body of Christ we receive the strength to live as citizens of heaven while we serve the earthly city.

quick: Matthew: the Pharisees and Herodians try to trap Jesus with a question about the tax to the emperor.
Jesus: give to the emperor what bears his image, and to God what bears God's image, that is, yourself.
Paul: all authority is from God; the ruler is God's servant for your good; pay taxes, not only from fear but for conscience.
2027-06-25.action: Put right one small dishonesty in your dealings with the government or the public this week, and pray for those who govern.
2027-06-25.question: Have I given to God what bears his image, my whole self?

family.explain: Some people wanted to trick Jesus with a question about money for the king. Jesus asked to see a coin. It had the king's picture on it. Jesus said: give the king what has his picture on it, and give God what belongs to God. What has God's picture on it? We do! God made each of us in his image. So we give our whole selves to God, and we are also good and honest citizens of our country.
family.intention: We pray for our country, for those who lead it, and for police officers, judges and all who serve the public.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one way our family can be honest and helpful to our town or village this week?”

illus: A village officer in central Kerala (a story told to illustrate the reading) was known in his office as the man who would not take anything extra. One day a contractor left an envelope on his table with a file. The officer pushed it back and said quietly, ‘The government already pays me for this.’ The man was annoyed: ‘Everyone takes it. You will gain nothing.’ The officer kept a small picture of the Sacred Heart in his drawer, and that evening he told his wife, ‘The coin has the government's stamp, but my hands have God's.’ Years later, when he retired, many people from the village came to the small function, among them that same contractor, who said in his speech, ‘He was the only officer whose signature I never had to buy.’

pm.open: Lord Jesus, you saw through every trap and spoke the truth with love. Gather us now, made in the image of God; teach us to give to God what is God's. Amen.
share: Whose head is this, and whose title? (Matthew 22:20). Whose image do I carry, and whom do I serve first?
Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s (Matthew 22:21). Am I honest in what I owe to the state and the public?
There is no authority except from God (Romans 13:1). How do I pray for and speak about those in authority?
Not only because of wrath but also because of conscience (Romans 13:5). Do I do right only when someone is watching?
pm.resp: Lord, all that we are is yours.
interc: For our country and all who govern it, that they may serve the common good with honesty and wisdom.
For civil servants, police officers and judges, that they may resist corruption and protect the weak.
For Christians who suffer for refusing to deny their faith, that they may stand firm like the apostles.
For young people preparing for public service and politics, that they may enter it with clean hands.
For ourselves, that we may be honest citizens and faithful children of God.
pm.close: Father, every person bears your image and belongs to you. Make us faithful in our duties to the earthly city and wholly yours in heart, until we reach the city that is to come. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, today some clever men try to trap Jesus. They ask him: should we pay taxes to the emperor or not? Whatever he answers, they think, he will be in trouble.
Jesus asks for a coin. Whose picture is on it? The emperor's. “Give therefore to the emperor the things that are the emperor’s, and to God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21).

The coin carries the emperor's image, so it goes back to him. But what carries God's image? You do. Every person is made in the image of God. So the coin may go to the government, but you yourself belong to God.

Saint Paul says that all authority comes from God, and that rulers are God's servants for our good (Romans 13:1, 4). So we pay our taxes, we keep the law, we vote with a good conscience, and we pray for those who govern. A Christian does not take or give bribes, even small ones.

But if any power commands what God forbids, we say with Peter and the apostles, “We must obey God rather than any human authority” (Acts 5:29). This week let us be honest citizens, and let us give back to God the only thing he asks for: our whole heart. Amen.
kids: Children, Jesus looked at a coin with the king's picture on it and said: give the king what has his picture. Then he meant something wonderful: God's picture is on you! You belong to God. So be honest, obey good rules, and give your whole heart to God!
